Preprint
PRECOCIAL: PRETRAINING WITH CODE CURRICU-
LUMS VIA ITERATIVE SEARCH FOR ACCELERATED
LEARNING
Edward Gu1
Ali Payani2
Kevin Ellis1
1Cornell University, 2Cisco Research
elg227@cornell.edu, apayani@cisco.com, kellis@cornell.edu
ABSTRACT
Fully synthetic pretraining data generated by symbolic programs can bootstrap
downstream training on naturalistic tasks, such as language modeling, but the gen-
erating programs have so far been designed by hand. We introduce PRECOCIAL,
a method for automatically optimizing programs that generate synthetic pretrain-
ing data. Starting from an initial generator program, an LLM iteratively rewrites
the program, and each rewrite is scored by pretraining a randomly-initialized
transformer on its data and fine-tuning it on the downstream task. Because ev-
ery score requires training, PRECOCIAL keeps a single network for the entire
search, continuing its pretraining for each accepted program instead of training a
new network per candidate, making it significantly more efficient. On four lan-
guage and code datasets, at a fixed fine-tuning budget, optimized programs reach
lower perplexity than hand-designed curricula, published procedural generators,
random program mutation and the program the LLM writes in the first iteration of
the search, and reach the same perplexity as the hand-designed curricula with 9–
33% fewer fine-tuning steps. PRECOCIAL also ends with lower perplexity than
FunSearch and AlphaEvolve, which train a new network for every candidate, at
the same number of evaluations and a lower cost. We also observe that an opti-
mized program generator from one domain transfers to datasets in other domains.
Additionally, optimized programs allow for better downstream performance on
four different reasoning and problem-solving tasks.
1
INTRODUCTION
Large Language Models (LLMs) begin as randomly-initialized transformer networks before pre-
training on masses of human data. Must training begin as a randomly-initialized blank slate? Bio-
logical learning suggests otherwise. From birth, wildebeests can run and spiders can weave webs,
drawing only on their genetic endowment: a compact discrete code (DNA) prewires useful behav-
iors and biases. Analogously, here we set out to discover compact symbolic programs which prime a
randomly-initialized transformer with useful inductive biases, which we call pretraining programs.
Previous work explores two families of pretraining programs: procedures which directly generate
weights and biases (Stanley et al., 2009; Barab´asi et al., 2023), and programs which generate syn-
thetic data (Zhang et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2026) for “pre-pretraining.” Both families could be fruit-
ful, but synthetic data is presently more practical and better-aligned with modern LLM pipelines, and
so we adopt it here (Figure 1). Recent work suggests that such pretraining programs can improve
both the sample and computational complexity of downstream learning: first training on cellular
automata, formal languages, or logical inferences then accelerates downstream learning in natural
language, visual reasoning, program source code, and more (Zhang et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025;
Jiang et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2026). In all of this work the program is designed by
hand. This prior literature naturally suggests our core research question: how could a pretraining
program be learned, synthesized, evolved, or automatically improved? This question also has im-
mediate implications for synthetic training data more broadly, as synthetic post-training has become
an important way of teaching language models to reason (Trinh et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025).

Figure 1: PRECOCIAL at a glance. Top: an LLM rewrites a program π (here, part of the program kept
for WikiText-103) whose data pretrains one transformer, continued across rewrites; a fine-tuned copy scores

validation perplexity by fine-tuning budget, solve rates, and the Sokoban puzzle of Figure 3.
To learn a pretraining program, we assume a collection of downstream datasets, such as natural
language corpora or reasoning problems. These downstream tasks define an objective for pretraining
programs, because we can measure how well a program’s synthetic data equips the learner to tackle
downstream data. Optimizing this objective is challenging for two reasons: the program search space
is discrete, and scoring a single program is expensive, since it requires pretraining a transformer on
the program’s data and then fine-tuning it on the downstream task. LLM-guided program search
such as FunSearch and AlphaEvolve (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025) score each
candidate independently, which is only affordable when the evaluation is cheap. Here, it would
mean pretraining a transformer from scratch for every candidate.
To address these challenges we introduce PRECOCIAL (PREtraining with COde Curriculums via
Iterative search for Accelerated Learning), a method for synthesizing and optimizing pretraining
programs. An LLM rewrites the program, each rewrite is scored by training on its data, and a rewrite
is kept only if it improves the downstream objective. To make each score cheap, PRECOCIAL keeps
a single network for the whole search: every accepted program continues pretraining the network
where the previous one left off, while a rejected program rolls back the checkpoint (Section 3.2).
Our goal is not to show that pretraining programs can help downstream tasks, which is already
well-established. Instead, our primary goal is to evaluate whether such pretraining programs can
be automatically optimized for a dataset of interest, and whether such optimization transfers across
datasets. This paper makes the following contributions:
• Algorithm. PRECOCIAL: LLM-guided search over pretraining programs whose fitness is
the downstream performance of a network trained on the program’s data (§3).
• Efficient continual pretraining. PRECOCIAL maintains a single model that is contin-
uously pretrained across candidate programs. At a fixed fine-tuning budget this is both
cheaper and better than training a fresh model per candidate (i.e. naive application of
FunSearch/AlphaEvolve): PRECOCIAL ends with lower perplexity than both while us-
ing 2.5× fewer pretraining steps (§4.3).
• Empirical validation. On four language and code datasets, optimized programs reach
lower perplexity than every other source of a curriculum we test (hand-written, procedural,
random mutation, the LLM’s first-iteration program) at every fine-tuning budget we mea-
sure, and they transfer to unseen datasets. At a 10k-step fine-tuning budget, PRECOCIAL
wins on all four reasoning and problem-solving tasks, and a Blocksworld search that never
sees the task does as well as one that does (§4).
2
BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK
Structural synthetic pretraining. A growing body of work shows that pretraining on structured
synthetic data teaches neural networks inductive biases that transfer to natural tasks. Cellular au-
2


--- Page 3 ---
Preprint
tomata at the edge of chaos yield models with strong compositional structure (Zhang et al., 2025);
neural cellular automata seed persistent memory circuits (Lee et al., 2026); and the phenomenon
extends to vision transformers (Shinnick et al., 2025). On the formal language side, Dyck languages
and context-free grammars teach bracket tracking and hierarchical composition (Hu et al., 2025;
Papadimitriou & Jurafsky, 2020), while LIME’s synthetic inference tasks aid compositional gen-
eralisation (Wu et al., 2021). A common theme is that abstract structural patterns, not semantic
content, drive transfer, and the benefit is usually one of efficiency: pre-pretraining on formal lan-
guages lets a 1B-parameter model reach the final loss of a model without it with 33% fewer tokens
(Hu et al., 2025), and procedural data lets models reach the same loss with 55–86% of the original
data (Jiang et al., 2026). This is also mostly what pretraining on real data buys: detectors trained
from scratch on COCO match ImageNet-pretrained ones once given a longer schedule (He et al.,
2019), and pretraining helps most, relative to the fine-tuning data, when that data is scarce (Her-
nandez et al., 2021). All of these generators are fixed by their designers. We compare against the
procedural generators of Jiang et al. (2026) directly, and report our gains in the same currency of
steps saved.
LLM-guided program search.
FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024) and AlphaEvolve
(Novikov et al., 2025) use LLMs as mutation operators over programs, maintaining populations
selected by black-box fitness, and are applied where a candidate is scored by running it. PRE-
COCIAL uses the same LLM-as-mutator paradigm, but its fitness requires training a network. We
therefore search over about ten candidates rather than thousands, keep one continually pretrained
network across them, and compare against both methods at the same budget.
Learning to generate training data. Generative Teaching Networks (Such et al., 2020) learn a
neural data generator by meta-gradients; Montessori-Instruct (Li et al., 2025) trains a teacher LLM
on instruction data using a student’s data influence; DataEvolve (Mi et al., 2026) evolves curation
strategies for natural pretraining data with trained models as fitness; CADEvolve (Elistratov et al.,
2026) evolves data-generating programs selected by validity checks; and Eurekaverse (Liang et al.,
2024) has an LLM write training environments scored by a reinforcement learner. Most closely
related, self-play pretraining (Cowsik et al., 2026) trains a transformer by reinforcement learning to
write programs for a universal Turing machine whose outputs lie at the frontier of what a learner can
learn, with no natural data. PRECOCIAL differs in two ways: it optimizes for downstream tasks,
whereas self-play is unsupervised, and it yields one compact program that describes the pretraining
distribution, whereas in self-play that distribution is defined by the weights of the generator network.
Our work is also related to meta-learning (Finn et al., 2017) and learned data augmentation (Ho et al.,
2019). We are not aware of prior work that searches over programs that generate pre-pretraining data
with the downstream performance of a network trained on that data as the fitness.
3
METHODS
Given a downstream dataset Ddown, our goal is to arrive upon a data generating program π whose
outputs prime a transformer to do well on that dataset, and potentially generalise to unseen down-
stream tasks as well. Each downstream dataset comprises train/val/test splits and a scoring metric,
(Dtrain, Dval, Dtest, L). We view each data generating program π as defining a distribution over token
sequences, and also view a downstream training split as a distribution over token sequences. We
write θ(D1, D2, . . . ) for the parameters of a transformer which is first trained on D1, then D2, etc.
Using this notation, we seek a program π optimising
ˆJ(π) = L(Dval, θ(π, Dtrain)),
(1)
where ˆJ approximates the true objective (which uses Dtest) on the validation data, ensuring that test
data is never seen during program search. We represent programs π in Python. Our transform-
ers are standard autoregressive models, except that we use byte-level tokenisation: tokenisers are
constructed from massive human data, and a key part of our problem statement is to arrive upon a
pretrained state without massive human data.
Figure 1 summarises the method; Figure 4 and Algorithm 1 in Appendix A give it with the notation
of this section and as pseudocode.
Initial program. An important choice is the starting point of the search. We construct a hand-written
program π0 by taking the union of existing synthetic pretraining paradigms from the recent literature
3

2. Cellular automata

Edge-of-chaos rules maximise transfer (Zhang et al., 2025)
3. Sequence ops

Set and sequence primitives (Wu et al., 2021)
4. Reasoning

(Table 1); it serves as a strong baseline. Programs follow a fixed generator contract (Appendix C):
each emits streams of abstract ASCII symbols, tagged with the rule that produced them; English
words are rejected by a validation step.
3.1
LLM-GUIDED SEARCH FOR PRETRAINING PROGRAMS
Following AlphaEvolve and others, PRECOCIAL generates variants of a program via LLM prompt-
ing and keeps the best under ˆJ. In the first iteration of the search, the LLM writes a program from
the generator contract, which lists the rule families of Table 1, and a sample of downstream data.
We call this the first-iteration program; it reflects the LLM’s prior, before feedback from training,
and 80–89% of the data in these programs comes from the rules of π0. At each subsequent round
the LLM receives the current accepted program, its objective value and the best so far, the valida-
tion curves of the last two candidates, 300 bytes of downstream training data, and returns a complete
rewritten program: it may reweight, remove, rewrite or invent rules freely (Appendix D). The rewrite
is scored by Eq. 1. It is accepted if ˆJ(πk) ≤ˆJ∗, the best value so far; otherwise the search reverts
to the last accepted program.
3.2
CONTINUAL PRETRAINING ACROSS CANDIDATES
Our objective function is very expensive to evaluate, requiring both pretraining and fine-tuning. This
is in stark contrast to most program synthesis problems, where evaluation is so fast that even guess-
and-check strategies are often viable (Li et al., 2022; Schkufza et al., 2013). After running this
expensive evaluation, a naive approach would throw away hard-won pretrained parameters before
generating and evaluating another program, as FunSearch and AlphaEvolve do when each candidate
is scored independently. Instead, PRECOCIAL continues pretraining the same model from the
last accepted checkpoint with each new program: the first program pretrains a randomly initialized
network for T0 steps, and every later candidate continues it for Tc < T0 steps. A rejected candidate’s
steps are discarded, so the network always reflects the accepted programs only. This can be viewed
as a form of continual learning, but also of curriculum learning: the system gradually enriches the
pretraining program, with each program resuming where the previous one left off. With T0=15k,
Tc=5k and ten candidates, a search performs 60k pretraining steps, against 150k for a fresh 15k-step
network per candidate.
Comparison to FunSearch and AlphaEvolve. Both maintain a population of programs from which
parents are sampled; PRECOCIAL is a single chain. We implement both as published, with a fresh
network trained for every candidate, at the same budget of ten evaluations (Appendix B).
4
EXPERIMENTS
4.1
SETUP
Downstream datasets. Language and code: TinyStories (Eldan & Li, 2023) (short narrative sto-
ries), WikiText-103 (Merity et al., 2017) (encyclopedia articles), CodeParrot (CodeParrot, 2022)
(Python source code) and CodeSearchNet (Husain et al., 2019) (Python functions), with 10k train-
ing documents each (TinyStories: 7,818 stories of at most 512 characters), byte-encoded as raw text,
and test sets from held-out data (Appendix E). Reasoning and problem solving: Blocksworld with
9 to 12 blocks, a standard benchmark of reasoning about actions for language models (Valmeekam
et al., 2023) (input: a PDDL problem; output: a plan, solved if replaying it in a simulator reaches the
goal); the 8-puzzle (states 10–20 moves from the goal); Sokoban (7×7, two boxes); and Countdown

with four numbers (Gandhi et al., 2024). Each has 5,000 training problems (Blocksworld 10,000)
and is scored by an exact checker on 500 test problems (Blocksworld 200), with greedy decoding.
Model training. We use small 0.69M-parameter GPT-2 models (3 layers, 4 heads, 128-dimensional
embeddings) with byte-level tokenization and a 512-byte context (1,024 for Blocksworld), opti-
mised with AdamW. A search runs K=10 rounds with T0=15k and Tc=5k steps on 2,000 synthetic
streams per round. Each candidate is fine-tuned for up to 10k steps with early stopping and ˆJ is val-
idation perplexity (on the answer tokens, for the puzzles). The LLM is Claude Sonnet 4 (Anthropic,
2025). The 10k-step budget and the ten rounds were set once and used unchanged for every dataset,
task and baseline (Appendix B).
Baselines. All share the architecture and training budget. Hand-written trains on π0 (Table 1).
Procedural trains on the published generators of Jiang et al. (2026). First iteration trains on the
first-iteration program (Section 3.1), the LLM’s program before any search, to tell whether the LLM
or the optimization drives the improvement. Random mutation runs the same loop with the LLM
replaced by random edits of that program (reweight all rules, remove one, or duplicate one). No
pretraining fine-tunes a randomly initialized network.
Matched pretraining. Comparing methods at the end of optimization would be confounded: a
rejected candidate is rolled back, so runs accumulate different amounts of pretraining (15k to 55k
steps across our runs). We therefore compare curricula under matched pretraining: the best program
of PRECOCIAL and of every baseline pretrains a fresh network for exactly 60k steps, then gets the
same fine-tuning and test: test perplexity after a 10k-step fine-tune for language, the exact checker
after a 10k-step fine-tune for puzzles (Appendix B). Section 4.3, which compares search procedures,
evaluates the network each search produces. We report mean ± SD over runs and two-sided t-tests
on paired differences.
4.2
LANGUAGE AND CODE: SEARCH AGAINST EVERY OTHER SOURCE OF A CURRICULUM
Table 2 compares PRECOCIAL with every other way of obtaining a curriculum. At the 10k-step
budget PRECOCIAL has the lowest test perplexity of any curriculum on all four datasets, and it is
level with no pretraining only on CodeParrot (3.207 against 3.204). Pooled over the four datasets, it
improves on the first-iteration program by 0.155 (lower in 30 of 36 paired runs), on random mutation
by 0.140 (32 of 36), on the hand-written program by 0.212 (31 of 36) and on procedural pretraining
by 0.371 (36 of 36), all with p<.001. Since the first-iteration and random-mutation baselines start
from the same program as the search, the gain over them is due to the LLM-guided search loop.
Program quality improves over the rounds: under matched pretraining the program kept after round
5 already beats the first-iteration program (round 0) by 0.126 (p=.005; 28 of 36), and the last four
rewrites add a further 0.029 (p=.07). On every dataset round 9 beats round 5, which beats round
0. Without matched pretraining, at the end of the ten-round loop, PRECOCIAL is again lowest on
every dataset (Appendix F.2). Figure 2 plots the search itself.
Across fine-tuning budgets (Figure 5 in Appendix F), PRECOCIAL is ahead of all four alternative
curricula at every budget from 2k to 20k steps, significantly so against every baseline at every budget
(Table 7). The lead is largest early, 0.78–1.55 perplexity at 2k steps, and narrows to 0.06–0.14 by
20k steps. Searching therefore buys downstream learning speed. Measured in fine-tuning steps, as
Hu et al. (2025) and Jiang et al. (2026) do, PRECOCIAL reaches its 2k-step perplexity with 57%,

4.3
PRECOCIAL AGAINST FUNSEARCH AND ALPHAEVOLVE
Naive application of FunSearch and AlphaEvolve to this setting would score every candidate on
a network pretrained from scratch for it, whereas PRECOCIAL continues one network across the
whole search (Section 3.2). We run all three at the same budget of ten evaluations on WikiText-
103 and CodeSearchNet, three seeds each, with everything else identical, including the GPU type
(Table 3). Table 3 shows the result. PRECOCIAL ends with lower test perplexity than both methods
on both datasets: averaged over the two, 0.231 below FunSearch (p=.15; lower in 4 of 6 paired runs)
and 0.296 below AlphaEvolve (p=.037; 5 of 6). It is also cheaper. FunSearch and AlphaEvolve
pretrain each of the ten candidates from random initialisation for T0=15k steps, 150k steps in total,
whereas PRECOCIAL pretrains one network for 15k steps and continues it by Tc=5k for each later
candidate, 60k in total. Fine-tuning is identical, so PRECOCIAL uses 19.5% and 17.1% less GPU
time per search, for about the same LLM bill; fine-tuning the candidates is the largest part of every
search, so the saving is modest here, and it grows with the number of candidates and with model
size (Appendix L). The continued network is what makes the difference: run with a fresh network
for every candidate, PRECOCIAL itself ends 0.244 perplexity higher (p=.055; 5 of 6). Part of the
gain is that the continued network accumulates more pretraining (up to 60k steps, against 15k for
each fresh network), a benefit obtained at lower cost.
4.4
TRANSFER TO UNSEEN DATASETS
Does a program optimized for one dataset help others? We take the network pretrained on the
WikiText-103 program of PRECOCIAL and of each baseline (matched pretraining) and fine-tune it
on TinyStories, CodeParrot and CodeSearchNet for 10k steps, with no further search (Table 4).
The program optimized for WikiText-103 transfers well to TinyStories and CodeParrot, where it
is the best curriculum and within 0.008 perplexity of a program optimized on the target itself, and

+0.090 (.036) +0.073 (.003) +0.005 (.104)
less well to CodeSearchNet. Pooled over the three targets it beats procedural pretraining (+0.224,
p=.011; 25 of 27 paired runs) and no pretraining (+0.484, p=.002), is ahead of the first-iteration
program (+0.095, p=.058) and random mutation (+0.188, p=.12), and is level with the hand-
written program (+0.035, p=.55). Transfer even crosses domains (Appendix F.3). The programs
optimized on Blocksworld and Sokoban (Section 4.5) do as well on the four language datasets as the
programs optimized on those datasets themselves (within 0.017 and 0.003 perplexity, p≥.69), and in
the other direction the WikiText-103 program solves more problems than the hand-written program
on all four reasoning tasks, though no single difference is significant. These tasks and language have
nothing in common at the task level, so this only makes sense if what transfers is the same structural
skill (nesting, sequence operations, state tracking) rather than anything task-specific.
4.5
REASONING AND PROBLEM SOLVING FROM SCRATCH
Do optimized programs help a small model learn tasks that require multi-step reasoning and problem
solving? Each task has three optimized programs (one per search seed), each trained with several
training seeds: three for Blocksworld (9 runs per method) and two for the others (6 runs per method).
Optimized programs beat the hand-written curriculum on all four tasks at the 10k-step fine-
tuning budget (Table 5): Sokoban +0.067 (p=.002), the 8-puzzle +0.073 (p=.005), Countdown
+0.025 (p=.025) and Blocksworld +0.196 (p=.033), ahead in every paired run on the first three.
Blocksworld is all-or-nothing: across the 33 runs of Table 5 every model that reaches a test perplexity
below 1.04 solves some problems and every model above it solves none (Appendix J), and 6 of 9
runs of the optimized programs land below that line, against 1 of 9 for the first-iteration program
and 2 of 9 for the hand-written program (Figure 8 in Appendix J). At this budget a network with no
synthetic pretraining learns almost nothing on the three tasks whose answer is a sequence of moves
(solve rates 0.000 on Blocksworld, 0.014 on the 8-puzzle and 0.007 on Sokoban).
The search loop matters, not only the LLM’s prior. Every search starts from the first-iteration
program, so comparing against it isolates what the rounds of search add. The optimized programs
beat it significantly on Sokoban (+0.073, p=.003) and the 8-puzzle (+0.090, p=.036), and lead
it on Blocksworld (+0.163, p=.06). On Sokoban the first-iteration program is no better than the
hand-written program, so the whole gain there comes from search. Countdown is the exception: its
first-iteration program is already close to the optimized program (+0.005, p=.10). The search adds

What the plans look like. Figure 3 shows plans written by one network of each method. On

4.6
WHAT THE LLM WRITES
Every program is a weighted set of named rules, each generating one kind of sequence. We classify
rules by name into content types (Appendix M) and measure, for each task, the share of synthetic
data coming from rules of the type that matches the task.
The LLM writes task-specific rules beyond the human-written π0. For example: precond
and state trans for Blocksworld, grid move and sokoban push for the move puzzles,
arith precedence for Countdown, func def and try catch for code. The first-iteration
programs contain almost none of this (0.0–8.4% of the data; Table 21 in Appendix M); the share
grows over the rounds of search (Figure 12) to 3.3–22.8%.
But task-specific content is not what the search selects for. Comparing, within each task and
round, the candidates the search accepted with those it rejected, accepted candidates carry no more
task-matching data (+2.2 points, stratified permutation test p=.35, 162 candidates). A direct test
agrees. We re-ran the Blocksworld search with the downstream data hidden from the LLM, which
then sees only its programs and their scores: it wrote no planning rules at all (0 of 298 added
rules), yet under matched pretraining its programs solve as many problems as those of the search
that sees the task (0.196 against 0.216, p=.82, 9 runs each). Much of what the search keeps is
general structure: the 28 generic rules of π0 (nesting, sequence operations and state tracking, among
others), which any byte-level sequence model can use, still produce 43–74% of the kept programs’
data, down from 80–89% in the first-iteration programs. This may explain why programs transfer
8


--- Page 9 ---
Preprint
across domains (Section 4.4): the puzzle programs that transfer best to language, Blocksworld and
Sokoban, carry the least task-specific data (3.3% and 12.3% of their kept programs, against 22.5%
and 22.8% for the 8-puzzle and Countdown), though four programs are too few to be sure.
5
DISCUSSION
We set out to ask whether a pretraining program can be optimized automatically, and at a fixed fine-
tuning budget our answer is yes. An LLM that rewrites a generator program, scored by training a
small network on the program’s data, finds programs that beat the hand-written curriculum, pub-
lished procedural generators, random mutation and its own first-iteration program on four language
and code datasets, and that beat the hand-written curriculum on four reasoning and problem-solving
tasks. The programs improve steadily over the rounds of search, and they transfer to datasets they
were not optimized on, in part even across domains.
What makes the search work. Our results point to the trained model rather than the LLM’s knowl-
edge of the task. On Blocksworld a search that never sees the task does as well as one that does,
and across tasks the programs the search accepts carry no more task-specific content than those it
rejects. The LLM is still not interchangeable with random edits: random mutation, which cannot
write new rules, falls short of it on language. Our reading is that the LLM’s job is to propose varied,
valid programs, including kinds of data the current program lacks, and that scoring each proposal on
a trained network is what decides which of them help. The same view accounts for transfer: much
of what survives is general structure that any sequence model can use.
Evaluating candidates when fitness requires training. Because every score requires training, how
candidates are evaluated matters as much as how they are proposed. Continuing one network across
candidates, instead of training a fresh network for each as FunSearch and AlphaEvolve do, is both
cheaper and better at a fixed budget.
When is this useful? Like other synthetic pretraining papers, the benefit we measure is efficiency:
the optimized programs reach a given perplexity in fewer fine-tuning steps (Table 8), and their lead
is largest with the least downstream data (Appendix G). PRECOCIAL is therefore aimed at settings
where downstream data is scarce and no more human data is available, since synthetic data costs
nothing to sample. And because programs transfer, a search can be run once and its program reused
on related datasets.
Connection to epiplexity. Epiplexity is the structural information that a computationally bounded
learner can extract from data, estimated by the area under its loss curve above the final loss (Finzi
et al., 2026). A pretraining program is a compact source of it, and PRECOCIAL produces new
epiplexity at every iteration: each rewrite gives the continued network new structure to learn, so its
pretraining loss rises at 32 of the 36 round boundaries of the language searches and falls again within
every round (Figure 7), and the search keeps the rewrites whose new structure helps downstream.
Across the 26 programs of this paper, the epiplexity a fresh 0.69M network extracts goes with lower
WikiText-103 perplexity (Spearman ρ=−0.64, p<.001) while the final pretraining loss does not, and
the optimized programs carry more of it than their first-iteration programs in all three WikiText-103
searches (Appendix I).
Limitations and future work. Our models are small (0.15M–3.36M parameters, Appendix G):
across that range the head start grows with the model but is spent sooner, so the lead at a fixed budget
shrinks with size. Larger models, larger downstream datasets and longer searches were beyond
our compute budget. Each task used three searches of ten evaluations with a single LLM (Claude
Sonnet 4), so smaller effects remain unresolved, and the task-hidden test was run on Blocksworld
only. Mixing different datasets together, and mixing the discovered pretraining data into fine-tuning,
may improve results further, especially for already pretrained models such as Llama or Qwen, where
replaying synthetic data could keep the model from forgetting what it has learned.
AI USE STATEMENT
In this work, the method itself uses a generative AI model: Claude Sonnet 4 writes and rewrites the
data generating programs during search (Section 3). We also used generative AI tools to implement
experiment code, run and analyse experiments, and assist in writing and editing the paper. All
9


--- Page 10 ---
Preprint
AI-assisted code, analyses and text were reviewed by the authors; every number in the paper is
computed by a script from the raw run logs. We take responsibility for the final content of this work,
including text, claims and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.
ETHICS STATEMENT
This work trains small models on public datasets (TinyStories, WikiText-103, CodeParrot and Code-
SearchNet) and on procedurally generated puzzles; it involves no human subjects or personal data,
and the synthetic pretraining data consists only of abstract symbols (Appendix C).
REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
The model, optimiser, search schedule and evaluation protocol are specified in Section 4.1 and
Appendix B; the generator contract and prompt in Appendices C and D; dataset sources and splits
in Appendix E. Code, all optimized programs and the script that computes every table from the run
logs will be released.

B
FURTHER EXPERIMENTAL SETUP DETAILS
Model.
Vocabulary 260 (256 bytes + PAD/BOS/EOS/SEP), 3 layers, 4 attention heads, 128-
dimensional embedding, 512-position context (1,024 for Blocksworld), ≈0.69M parameters. All
weights are randomly initialised; embeddings are not reinitialised between pretraining and fine-
tuning.
Pretraining. 2,000 streams per round, 50 sentences per stream, truncated to the context length.
Round 0: 15,000 steps from scratch; later rounds: 5,000 continued steps from the last accepted
checkpoint. A ten-round search therefore performs 60,000 pretraining steps, and its kept network
carries between 15,000 and 60,000 of them, depending on how many rounds were accepted. Batch
size 8, AdamW, learning rate 3 × 10−4, gradient clipping at 1.0.
Fine-tuning. Up to 10,000 steps, learning rate 3×10−4, batch size 8, early stopping with patience 5
evaluations every 500 steps; the checkpoint with the lowest validation perplexity is tested. A second,
longer fine-tune of the kept pretrained network (early stopping with patience 10; every run continued
well past 20k steps) supplies the validation curve from which we read the best perplexity reached
within each fine-tuning budget from 2k to 20k steps (Figures 5 and 6, Appendix F). For the puzzles
the loss and the perplexity are computed on the answer tokens only.
Choice of budgets. A search evaluates ten candidates, each with its own pretraining and fine-tuning,
so each evaluation must be short. We fine-tune for 10k steps (about eight passes over a 10k-document
training set at batch size 8), which keeps a ten-candidate search under one GPU-hour on the 0.69M
model (Appendix L). It is a budget, not convergence: validation perplexity is still falling at 10k steps
in 96% of the fine-tunes run during our searches. Because the search’s fitness is measured at this
budget, results at 10k steps evaluate exactly what the search optimizes; Figure 5 and Table 7 report
2k to 20k steps as well. Ten rounds keep the LLM cost near $1 per search, and the program kept
after round 5 already captures most of the gain (Table 2), so more rounds would add little. Both
values were set once, before the experiments reported here, and used unchanged for every dataset,
task, baseline and model size.
Search. Ten rounds; a candidate is accepted if its validation perplexity is no worse than the best so
far (tolerance 0), and otherwise both the program and the pretrained checkpoint are rolled back. The
LLM (Claude Sonnet 4 via the OpenRouter API) samples the first-iteration program at temperature
0.9 and rewrites at temperature 0.7. FunSearch uses 4 islands and prompts with the best programs of
one island; AlphaEvolve uses one database, fitness-proportional parent sampling and 2 inspiration
programs per prompt. As published, both pretrain a fresh network from random initialisation for
every candidate (15,000 steps, then the fine-tuning above). All three methods make one LLM call
per evaluation, plus a retry whenever a returned program fails validation.
Matched pretraining. For every comparison of curricula (Tables 2, 5 and 4), the kept program
of PRECOCIAL and of every baseline pretrains a fresh network for exactly 60,000 steps on 2,000
streams, followed by the fine-tuning above. For language, each of the three kept programs per
method (one per search seed) is trained with three training seeds, the search seed and two others,
giving 9 runs per cell of Tables 2 and 4; no pretraining uses the same nine training seeds, and runs are
paired by training seed. Blocksworld is fine-tuned for the full 10,000 steps without early stopping:
its validation perplexity plateaus early, and patience-5 stopping ends fine-tuning at 1,000 to 3,500
steps, above the perplexity at which plans start to succeed (Appendix J).
C
GENERATOR PROGRAM SPECIFICATION
The generator contract requires programs to define:
def generate_stream(num_sentences: int) -> List[Tuple[str, str]]:
"""Returns list of (rule_name, content_string) pairs.
content_string must use only abstract ASCII symbols."""
All content strings are drawn from the following vocabulary: uppercase letters (A–Z), digits (0–9),
brackets (()[]<>{}), operators (+-*/=ˆ%˜), separators (|;,.!@#$ ), and arrows (->, =>).
English words and multi-character token names are forbidden by a validation step that checks for
13


--- Page 14 ---
Preprint
common English words before accepting any generated program. The rule name returned with each
content string tags the stream and is used for the rule analysis (Section 4.6).
D
PROMPT STRUCTURE
First iteration. The LLM is asked to design synthetic pretraining data for a small GPT-2 model
whose transformer layers (not its token embeddings’ meaning) will transfer to the downstream task,
and receives the generator contract, which lists the rule families of Table 1 with their literature
justifications, the task type, and 500 bytes of downstream training data.
Each later round. The prompt contains, in order: (1) the round number and a note that the network
is continued from the previous round rather than retrained; (2) the current validation perplexity and
the best so far; (3) the validation perplexity along the fine-tuning curves of the current and previous
candidates; (4) 300 bytes of downstream training data; (5) the current program in a Python code
fence; (6) the generator contract; and (7) the instruction: add any number of new rule types, remove
any rules that are unhelpful, and modify existing generators and their weights, with no cap on the
size of the change (the prompt notes, as information only, that large distribution shifts can cause
forgetting in a continually trained network). The LLM returns the complete program. For the task-
hidden ablation (Section 4.6) the downstream sample is replaced by a notice that it is withheld.

THE TEN-ROUND LOOP WITHOUT MATCHED PRETRAINING
The tables below evaluate each method with the network its own ten-round loop produced, instead
of retraining its kept program on a fresh network. Methods then differ in accumulated pretraining:
the kept checkpoints carry 42,500 pretraining steps on average for PRECOCIAL against 37,100–
38,800 for the baselines. PRECOCIAL is lowest on every dataset, and every pooled difference is
significant.

G
MODEL SIZE AND DOWNSTREAM DATA SIZE
Both sweeps use WikiText-103 with raw text and evaluate the network each method’s ten-round
loop produced (as in Appendix F.2, not matched pretraining). Every model size runs the same
search schedule on 2,000 synthetic streams per round.
Model size. Table 13 repeats the WikiText-103 comparison at 0.15M, 0.69M and 3.36M parameters,
and Figure 6 follows the lead over no pretraining across fine-tuning budgets. The head start is
larger for larger models but comes earlier: at its peak a network with no synthetic pretraining trails
PRECOCIAL by 1.44 perplexity at 0.15M (after 5k fine-tuning steps), 2.83 at 0.69M (after 2k) and
3.56 at 3.36M (after 1k). A larger model also closes the gap sooner, so at the 10k-step budget of
Table 13 the lead shrinks with size: over the hand-written curriculum it falls from 1.445 to 0.196
and 0.098 perplexity, and over no pretraining from 1.248 to 0.273 and 0.195. With three seeds none
of these differences is significant on its own (p between .076 and .351). The synthetic budget is the
same for every size, so larger models receive less synthetic data per parameter; whether a curriculum
scaled with the model keeps the lead is untested.
Table 13: Model size sweep, N=10k WikiText-103 documents: test perplexity after a 10k-step fine-tune,
mean ± SD over 3 seeds. Last two columns: seed-paired differences (positive: PRECOCIAL lower), p in
parentheses.

Figure 7: Pretraining loss during the search, concatenated over rounds (mean over 3 seeds); the x axis is
thousands of pretraining steps. From round 1 on, PRECOCIAL sits above the first-iteration and random-
mutation baselines (in round 0 all three train on the same first-iteration program) and spikes at each round
boundary, where the next candidate changes the data, yet reaches the best downstream perplexity (Table 9).
17


--- Page 18 ---
Preprint
In Figure 7, from round 1 on PRECOCIAL’s pretraining loss is higher than that of the first-iteration
and random-mutation baselines on all four datasets, and in the last round it is also higher than the
hand-written program’s on three of them (on WikiText-103 the hand-written program ends with
the highest pretraining loss of any method), while PRECOCIAL’s downstream perplexity is the
lowest everywhere. Part of the gap is mechanical: the first-iteration and hand-written programs
show the network the same distribution in every round, and random mutation only reweights, drops
or duplicates the first-iteration program’s rules, whereas an LLM rewrite can add new kinds of data.
This is also what produces the sawtooth: PRECOCIAL’s loss rises at 32 of its 36 round boundaries.
We therefore report the pattern without claiming that the optimized data is intrinsically harder to fit;
separating “harder data” from “newer data” would need a run that replays the optimized programs
in a fixed order.
I
EPIPLEXITY OF THE PROGRAMS
We estimate the epiplexity of a program’s data with the prequential estimate of Finzi et al. (2026).
A fresh 0.69M network, with the architecture and optimiser of our experiments, makes a single pass
over 40,000 newly generated streams of the program (5,000 steps of 8 streams, each truncated to
512 tokens), so that no stream is seen twice. Before each update we record the mean per-token loss
ℓt on the batch; after the pass we measure the loss H on 500 held-out streams of the same program,
which estimates its time-bounded entropy. The epiplexity estimate is S = P
t(ℓt −H), the area
between the loss curve and the final loss, in nats per token summed over steps. Table 15 gives S and
H for the 26 programs of this paper. Across them, more epiplexity goes with lower WikiText-103
test perplexity after matched pretraining and a 10k-step fine-tune (Spearman ρ = −0.64, p < .001;
the perplexity of the run whose training seed is the program’s search seed, or the mean of three runs
for the hand-written and procedural programs), whereas H does not predict perplexity (ρ = −0.08,
p = .69). The optimized WikiText-103 programs carry more epiplexity than their first-iteration
programs in all three searches (1659 against 1590, 1459 against 1397 and 1396 against 1293), and
every group of LLM-written programs carries more on average than the hand-written and procedural
programs. Epiplexity separates these broad sources of programs better than it ranks the programs of
one search: the program kept after round 5 has more epiplexity than the final program in two of the
three WikiText-103 searches, although the final programs reach lower perplexity (Table 2).
Table 15: Epiplexity S (nats per token summed over steps) and final held-out loss H (nats per token) of each
program’s synthetic data, measured with a fresh 0.69M network making one pass over 40,000 fresh streams.
Mean and range over the programs of a group; all programs except the last group come from the WikiText-103
searches.

Figure 8: Every matched-pretraining run of Table 5 (dots; bars: means). On Blocksworld the solve rate is
nearly all-or-nothing: it is a step function of the test perplexity the fine-tuned model reaches (Table 17), so
single runs sit at zero or well above it.
Blocksworld is nearly all-or-nothing. A plan is about 30 actions (31 on average for our test prob-
lems) and every action must be legal and correct, so a model either produces whole correct plans
often or almost never. Across the 33 Blocksworld runs of Table 5 the solve rate is a step function
of the test perplexity the fine-tuned model reaches (Table 17; Spearman ρ = −0.78 over 33 runs,
p = 6.5 × 10−8): all 9 runs below 1.04 solve some problems (0.015 to 0.635) and all 24 runs above
it solve none, with no run in between. This is why single Blocksworld runs sit either at zero or far
above it (Figure 8), and why we use 9 runs per method there. Table 16 gives the perplexities behind
those solve rates.

K
THE PLANS OF FIGURE 3
The networks of Figure 3 were trained for the figure with the protocol of Table 5: each method’s
matched-pretrained network is fine-tuned on the task with training seed 64, and its greedy plan for
every test puzzle is replayed by the task’s exact checker. Besides the methods of Table 5, the figure
shows a universal prior: a network pretrained with the same model and budget on the outputs of
random programs for a Brainfuck-like universal machine, our reimplementation after Grau-Moya
et al. (2024). The puzzle shown for each task is chosen by a fixed rule, not by hand: among the test
puzzles that the PRECOCIAL network solves (119 of 500 for the 8-puzzle, 43 of 500 for Sokoban
and 82 of 200 for Blocksworld), keep those solved by the fewest of the other networks trained
for the figure, and take the first in test-set order. The other networks are those shown and four
more pretrained on reimplementations of published synthetic data (procedural generators, Dyck
languages, cellular automata and LIME-style tasks), and for Blocksworld also random mutation;
for every task the fewest is zero, and 38, 21 and 20 puzzles qualify. Figures 9–11 show six evenly
spaced states of each plan. Table 18 gives the solve rates of these networks over three training seeds;
they are separate runs from those of Table 5.

and add up to the total (up to rounding). How to read each column is explained below the table.

Reading Table 19. Each row is one way of running a search that evaluates ten candidate programs.
Pretraining steps is the number of synthetic pretraining steps summed over the whole search, not
a fine-tuning budget: PRECOCIAL pretrains one network for 15k steps for the first candidate and
continues it for 5k steps for each of the nine later ones (15k + 9×5k = 60k), whereas FunSearch
and AlphaEvolve as published pretrain a fresh network for 15k steps for each of the ten candidates
(10×15k = 150k). The five time columns split one search into synthetic pretraining; fine-tuning
the ten candidates for up to 10k steps each, which is identical under both protocols; waiting for the
LLM; everything else (generating the synthetic data, evaluation and bookkeeping); and their total,
mean ± SD over the six searches. LLM calls counts every call, including retries of programs that
failed validation, and API cost prices them at Claude Sonnet 4 rates. Test ppl is the test perplexity
of the program each search kept after a 10k-step fine-tune, averaged over the six searches (three on
each dataset). One network cuts pretraining time by 59–61%, but fine-tuning is unchanged and takes
42–53% of a search, so the total falls by 17.1–19.5%.
Longer searches and larger models (projection). From the WikiText-103 searches of Appendix G
(3 per model size, RTX A6000), one candidate costs 0.039 GPU-h of fine-tuning at 0.69M parame-
ters and 0.067 at 3.36M, one LLM call 0.015, and everything else 0.003, while synthetic pretraining
costs 2.54 GPU-h (0.69M) and 5.07 (3.36M) per million steps. With one network a search of n
candidates pretrains 15k + 5k (n−1) steps; with a fresh network per candidate, 15k n. Table 20
multiplies these rates out. These are projections, not runs. At ten candidates they reproduce the
measured one-network searches (0.73 against 0.71 GPU-h at 0.69M, 1.15 against 1.18 at 3.36M),
but they predict a 24% saving at 0.69M against the 17–20% measured in Table 19, so they overstate
21


--- Page 22 ---
Preprint
the saving somewhat. The saving grows with the number of candidates and with model size, because
pretraining is a larger share of each candidate’s cost for a larger model.

M
RULE CLASSIFICATION
Rules are classified by keyword matching on their names, which are the LLM’s own and usu-
ally say what the rule does: planning (e.g. pddl, plan, action, state, precond, grid,
move, puzzle, sokoban), arithmetic (arith, expr, math, fraction, make24), code syn-
tax (func, class def, import, method, param, try catch), list and string operations,
logic, cellular automata, and formal structure (nest, dyck, tree, cfg, stack); a name takes the
first matching type in a fixed order. The share of a type is its fraction of the synthetic data generated
in a round, by volume. The classifier is a keyword map, so single percentages are approximate; the
script that assigns every name is released with the code.
